newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Jackie McLean's sound echoes years in jazz.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Jackie McLean's sound echoes years in jazz.

text.p: Saxophonist Jackie McLean was on stage at the Kennedy Centre reminiscing about growing up in Harlem, when he studied with bebop legend Bud Powell, first heard tenorman Dexter Gordon and tagged along with Charlie Parker to the funeral of trumpeter Hot Lips Page.

He has had a rich life, much of it mirroring the history of jazz over the past several decades. But the talk at his recent concert would have amounted to no more than an interesting biographical sketch if not for his playing, where his personality came alive. As Billy Taylor, the pianist and now host for a National Public Radio series on jazz, said in introducing McLean: "He plays with passion and with heart."

McLean walks out on stage to resounding applause, takes the mouthpiece off his alto and after a quick count begins to play, hunching his shoulders and bending his neck into his sound. When he is playing hard and fast, his body expresses the tension of his music. His sax sounds tough and gritty. He fills the air with soulful arpeggios.

He drags behind the beat slightly, then jumps ahead of it quick time, his knees buckling with the rhythm, playing on the edge of a note so that he almost sounds out of tune. These are the devices he uses to bring you into his world.

And when you are ready catch your breath on a heartfelt ballad, he does not let go. He brings a raw bluesy edge to the most romantic tune, never stopping at its innocence, always finding the painful undercurrents.

Just listen to "A Cottage for Sale" on his recent release for Blue Note, "Hat Trick," his latest in a recording career that stretches back to 1951 when he first appeared as a sideman on Miles Davis's recording "Dig." He was all bebop back then but now his sound is deeper, more personal, full of blues and racy squalls.
Asked about his sound, McLean told Reuters: "It's like a diamond that you keep polishing, it's a spiritual thing." And he left it at that.

McLean, 65, grew up with an extraordinary bunch of street corner friends like drummer Art Taylor and tenor giant Sonny Rollins, who helped define jazz in the post-bebop era. When the 52nd Street scene in New York was in full swing, McLean used to try to sneak into jazz clubs to hear his idols like Parker, who eventually became his friend.

He owes his sound to the great tenor players like Lester Young, Dexter Gordon and Don Byas whom he tried to mimic, arriving at a full and throaty sound on the higher alto that is unique. While Bud Powell taught him chord changes and the blues, Parker became a mentor and close friend and Bird's influence is still palpable. He wears two neck straps when he plays: "Maybe it sounds a little corny, but I put one on the horn and one on for Bird."
But it was not until he played with Charles Mingus in the 1950s that he found his own sound under the force of Mingus' will. From that period on, McLean delved into his own ideas.

He tapped into hard bop in the late '50s, experimented with free jazz in the 1960s and then moved from New York to Hartford to found a jazz programme at the Hartt School of Music. Since then, he has mentored a steady stream of talented jazz musicians.

Now approaching his golden years, McLean has stepped up the performance pace, touring regularly, performing in New York clubs and recently issuing the recording on the Blue Note label where he made a series of memorable LPs more than 30 years ago. He has appeared on independent and major labels throughout the years.
His fans -- a hard-core cadre that seems to show up at all his venues -- appear pleased with the new activity. One in Japan even insisted the saxophonist autograph his cashmere coat, McLean said.

Often when he appears live, McLean will play Thelonious Monk's classic "'Round Midnight" and he and Taylor explored it again in Washington. It might well be a signature tune for McLean, for he always delves deeply into its meaty chords and angular rhythms -- never content to play it like the standard it has become.
"''Round Midnight' is one of the toughest songs I've ever learned how to play," McLean told the audience that night. "I'm still learning how to play it." Like the man, the music is still developing.
